title: AsterBank Security Review - Offline installs / signed bundles (Redwood Private)
topics: Offline / air-gapped install workflow for Redwood Private
Supply chain integrity: manifest, hashes, signature verification
Signing keys: custody, rotation, revocation, trust roots
Audit logs: local events, export to SIEM, retention
summary: AsterBank reviewed Redwood’s planned/ongoing approach for signed offline bundles for Redwood Private installs in air-gapped environments. Key questions focused on (1) how Redwood proves integrity/provenance without network access, (2) signing key custody and rotation (including how customers update trust roots offline), (3) audit log evidence (local-only logging + SIEM export), (4) replay/downgrade protections, and (5) documented exceptions/break-glass. Redwood agreed to share a draft bundle verification guide, key rotation/runbook excerpts, and a sample audit event schema and support bundle output. AsterBank requested clarity on algorithm choices/FIPS posture and a written statement about fail-closed behavior when the key is unknown or signature invalid.
next_steps: Redwood to send AsterBank: signed offline bundle workflow one-pager + verification CLI examples (preflight / inspect).
Redwood to provide: key custody + rotation overview (including how trust store updates work offline) and revocation approach.
Redwood to share: sample local audit events for verification success/failure and how to export to SIEM in Private.
AsterBank to confirm crypto requirements (FIPS constraints, allowed curves/algorithms) and preferred time source guidance for air-gapped hosts.
Schedule follow-up 30 min to review documents + answer remaining supply chain questions.
action_items: Owner: Fatima Noor | Item: Send draft 'Air-gapped install + verify signatures' steps + expected outputs (preflight/inspect) | Due: 2025-10-24
Owner: Marcus Lin | Item: Provide security FAQ responses: integrity/provenance story, fail-closed policy, replay/downgrade mitigations | Due: 2025-10-27
Owner: Olga Petrov | Item: Share controls/evidence mapping for signing + audit logs (SOC2-style narrative) suitable for TPRM | Due: 2025-10-29
Owner: Tom Wexler (AsterBank) | Item: Confirm crypto policy (FIPS mode expectations, allowed algos) and time sync constraints in air-gap | Due: 2025-10-31
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-10-22
Start time: 3:00 PM ET
Duration: 58 minutes
Call type: Security review

Attendees
Redwood: Markus Klein, Fatima Noor, Marcus Lin, Olga Petrov
AsterBank: Priya Nair, Tom Wexler, Elena Markovic, Samir Qureshi


[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Alright, folks, thanks for making time. Goal today is to walk through how Redwood Private is going to work for offline installs, specifically the signed bundle stuff, and then answer all the supply chain questions. Priya, do you want to start with what you need out of this for your review?

[00:24] Priya Nair: Yeah. Thanks, Markus. We’re trying to close out third-party risk for the on-prem deployment. Our main concerns are: how do we know what we install is what you built, because we can’t call back to your services. And second, key management—who has the signing keys, how are they rotated. Third, auditability, like, we need evidence logs locally.

[00:53] Elena Markovic: And I’ll add, we’ll need written statements. Like, do you fail closed. If signature fails, is it blocked. If key is unknown, is it blocked. That kind of thing.

[01:06] Markus Klein: Yep. Makes sense. Fatima, you want to level set on the workflow? Then Marcus can get into the security bits.

[01:14] Fatima Noor: Sure. So the offline flow is basically: you receive an offline bundle—think tarball—containing the installer bits, the charts/manifests, and references to all required container images and runtime/model artifacts. In the bundle there’s a manifest listing every artifact with a hash. That manifest is signed by Redwood. On the air-gapped machine, you run a preflight command that verifies the signature, verifies the manifest hashes match the bundle contents, and only then allows install.

[01:49] Tom Wexler: When you say “only then,” do you mean the installer literally refuses to proceed?

[01:54] Fatima Noor: Correct. By default it blocks. You’ll get a failure with a reason code and a log path.

[02:01] Priya Nair: OK, what is the signature format? Like PGP, X.509, Sigstore? We can’t depend on external transparency logs in air gap.

[02:12] Marcus Lin: Yeah, good question. We’re not requiring an online transparency service for the verification step. The important thing is you have a trust root locally—basically Redwood’s public signing key(s) in a trust store. Verification is fully offline. We sign a canonical representation of the manifest. The signature is detached, so you’ll see something like manifest.json and manifest.sig.

[02:35] Samir Qureshi: Detached signature is fine. What about the algorithm? Also we have FIPS constraints. We can’t use like random new stuff.

[02:44] Marcus Lin: Understood. The plan is to stick to widely supported primitives. We’ll confirm exact algorithm details in writing—what we’re targeting is a standard scheme supported by common crypto libraries and amenable to FIPS-validated modules in customer environments. The installer itself uses OS crypto primitives where possible. We can align on what you allow—RSA vs ECDSA, that kind of decision.

[03:11] Priya Nair: I’ll be very direct: we will want either RSA-3072 or ECDSA P-256, depending on our internal policy. Ed25519 is usually a no for our regulated apps, unless there’s a FIPS story.

[03:24] Marcus Lin: Got it. We’ll take that as an action item. We can support a set; the critical thing is the trust store / rotation process doesn’t brick your installs.

[03:38] Elena Markovic: Can you describe key custody? Who can sign, where is the private key, is there a ceremony, approvals?

[03:47] Olga Petrov: I can speak to that at a high level. Signing keys are controlled by Release Engineering with Security oversight. There’s a documented key ceremony, limited operators, separation of duties, and audit evidence. Signing happens in the release pipeline under protected conditions—approvals, restricted role, and logging. We can share our narrative for customer questionnaires.

[04:13] Elena Markovic: OK. Does any engineer have access to the private key? Because that’s usually the red flag.

[04:19] Olga Petrov: No, not “any engineer.” Access is limited to designated signing operators and requires approvals. Also, we can provide attestation about how we protect the key material. Details might be summarized, but we’ll give enough for TPRM.

[04:34] Tom Wexler: On the bundle contents: you mentioned container images. Are images inside the tarball, or do we pull from a registry? Because we can’t.

[04:43] Fatima Noor: In air-gapped mode, you don’t pull. The bundle includes either the images themselves or an export that you load into your internal registry. The manifest lists digests and expected hashes, so the installer can validate you loaded the right thing. In practice, teams bring the bundle in on removable media and load into an internal Harbor/Artifactory registry.

[05:06] Tom Wexler: OK, so it’s like “docker load” but for containerd or whatever.

[05:11] Fatima Noor: Exactly. (And sorry, I might say “docker” generically.) We have commands for containerd and CRI-O too.

[05:20] Priya Nair: Let’s talk about “proves what you built.” Are you doing build provenance? SLSA? Or is it just “we sign it.”

[05:29] Marcus Lin: The initial guarantee is integrity and provenance via signing: the signed manifest binds together the artifact list and hashes. If anything is modified in transit, verification fails. For build provenance, we can provide a statement of our build controls and reproducibility goals. We also include references to SBOM artifacts so you can validate components offline. We’re working toward stronger provenance attestation, but we don’t want to depend on online systems for your verification.

[05:57] Samir Qureshi: SBOM—what format? CycloneDX, SPDX?

[06:01] Marcus Lin: We can provide an SPDX or CycloneDX output depending on component. The important thing is the manifest contains a pointer to the SBOM file plus a hash. So the SBOM you read is the SBOM that was produced and included in the signed bundle.

[06:18] Priya Nair: OK. Downgrade attacks. If someone replays an older but validly signed bundle, they can bring back vulnerabilities. How do you prevent that?

[06:29] Marcus Lin: Yep. There are two layers. One, we include the bundle version and build ID in the signed manifest. Two, the installer maintains local install state—so it knows “current installed version.” If you try to install a lower version, it blocks by default unless an explicit rollback procedure is invoked. Rollbacks are controlled and logged.

[06:55] Tom Wexler: But in an air gap, how does it know “latest?”

[06:58] Marcus Lin: It doesn’t know “latest” globally. It knows “not older than what’s on this cluster.” So it prevents downgrade relative to your own state. If you’re bootstrapping a new cluster, there isn’t prior state, so you’re effectively deciding what to install—but you’re still protected against tampering.

[07:19] Elena Markovic: That’s acceptable. We’ll document procedural controls for new clusters.

[07:26] Priya Nair: Another corner: signature validity windows. If you use certs with “not before / not after,” air-gapped time can drift. We’ve seen vendors brick installs because time is wrong.

[07:40] Marcus Lin: Yep, time skew in air-gapped environments is a known issue. We try to avoid fragile dependencies on accurate system time for basic verification. Where time is used, we document the requirement and provide troubleshooting guidance. Also, we can provide a diagnostic mode that reports time skew clearly. But default behavior stays fail-closed.

[08:05] Samir Qureshi: “Diagnostic mode” meaning override?

[08:08] Marcus Lin: Not exactly. There are two different things. One is diagnostic output—like print what time the host thinks it is versus what the signature expects. Another is break-glass override, which is a policy-gated “proceed despite verification failure” path. That would be used only in exceptional cases, heavily logged, and typically requires approval.

[08:31] Priya Nair: We need that documented. If you have an override, we need to know what’s logged and how you prevent it from being the normal way.

[08:40] Markus Klein: Totally. We’ll share the break-glass process doc. It’s basically: explicit flag, plus it emits an audit warning event, and Support asks for justification and sign-off depending on severity.

[08:55] Elena Markovic: So you have a support-based approval? Is it enforced technically?

[09:01] Marcus Lin: Some enforcement is technical, like it requires a specific flag and can be disabled via config policy. Some is process/policy. In offline deployments, you ultimately control the machine, so we focus on: (a) safe default is blocked, (b) override is noisy and leaves evidence.

[09:21] Tom Wexler: Let’s get into audit logs. We need to show an auditor “we verified vendor signature” and “here are the results.” What do you log, and where?

[09:30] Fatima Noor: The installer writes local logs to disk, and also emits structured audit events. In Private deployments, those events can be stored locally and optionally exported to your SIEM if you run the exporter.

[09:44] Kevin—sorry Marcus, is it you? Who owns audit events.

[09:48] Marcus Lin: Kevin leads the SIEM requirements normally, but today it’s me. The audit event includes fields like: event type “bundle_verification,” outcome success/failure, reason code (hash_mismatch, signature_invalid, unknown_key, expired/not_yet_valid), bundle build ID, bundle version, and the key identifier used. We avoid logging sensitive file contents—just metadata.

[10:18] Priya Nair: Key identifier meaning like a fingerprint?

[10:21] Marcus Lin: Exactly, a key ID or fingerprint so you can tie it to the trusted key in your trust store.

[10:28] Samir Qureshi: Where is this trust store physically? Embedded in the installer binary? File on disk? Both?

[10:35] Marcus Lin: It can be packaged with the installer and also allow an external trust store file path. The reason is rotation: you might need to update keys without reinstalling the entire installer. But we also include defaults for “works out of the box.”

[10:54] Tom Wexler: Rotation is my biggest concern. Suppose you rotate signing keys. Our environment cannot reach out to fetch new keys. How do we update trust roots offline?

[11:06] Marcus Lin: We provide a trust store update package as part of the offline distribution story. So you’d receive the new public key(s) via the same controlled channel as bundles—typically included in a bundle or as a separate signed update. During a transition window, the installer trusts multiple keys: old + new. You update your trust store before you install bundles signed by the new key.

[11:35] Elena Markovic: How do we know that trust store update itself is legitimate?

[11:39] Marcus Lin: Great catch. We sign trust store updates as well—using an existing trusted root. Essentially, you need an initial trust anchor. After that, updates are chained. We’ll provide a rotation runbook so it’s predictable and doesn’t create outages.

[12:03] Priya Nair: OK. What’s your revocation story? If you think a signing key is compromised.

[12:09] Marcus Lin: In an offline world, revocation is tricky because you can’t “phone home.” Our approach: (1) publish an emergency key rotation and communicate out-of-band, (2) ship an updated trust store that removes/blocks the compromised key and adds replacement keys, (3) make installer treat the compromised key as untrusted once updated. For customers in air gap, there’s a manual operational step to import updated trust store.

[12:38] Priya Nair: So the requirement is: we must apply the trust store update to stop trusting the old key.

[12:43] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[12:46] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable, but we’ll need it in a control: “trust store updates applied within X days.”

[12:52] Olga Petrov: We can support that with guidance and customer comms templates.

[13:00] Tom Wexler: On the manifest canonicalization: JSON can be tricky. Are you signing raw JSON bytes? Because whitespace changes would break signature.

[13:09] Marcus Lin: Exactly why we have canonicalization rules. We don’t sign “whatever”; we sign a canonical form—stable ordering, stable encoding. That prevents accidental breakage. Also, the manifest includes hash algorithm identifiers.

[13:26] Samir Qureshi: Hash algorithm: sha256? sha512?

[13:29] Marcus Lin: Today we’re using SHA-256 as baseline. If you need SHA-384/512 for policy reasons, that’s a discussion, but SHA-256 is common and generally accepted.

[13:40] Priya Nair: It’s accepted for integrity. Fine.

[13:43] Markus Klein: Priya, are there any concerns about where the installer gets dependencies? Like, does it ever try to download anything?

[13:51] Tom Wexler: Yes. We need guarantee it does not attempt outbound network. Our environment flags that.

[13:58] Fatima Noor: In offline mode, outbound fetch is disabled. The installer checks required artifacts exist in the bundle and local registry, and it fails if anything is missing rather than downloading. We can show you the config that enforces “no egress.”

[14:16] Priya Nair: Great.

[14:18] Elena Markovic: Evidence: do you have SOC 2? ISO? We’re mostly focused on SDLC and release integrity.

[14:25] Olga Petrov: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. For this specific feature, we’re documenting the signing process as part of release controls. We can provide the SOC summary under NDA and a specific narrative for “artifact signing control.”

[14:42] Elena Markovic: Fine.

[14:45] Priya Nair: I want to drill into “what exactly is signed.” Is it only the manifest, or each artifact individually?

[14:55] Marcus Lin: We sign the manifest, and the manifest contains hashes for each artifact. That’s equivalent from an integrity perspective, as long as the manifest is comprehensive and verification checks every hash. It avoids needing multiple signature files. Some components like chart tarballs also have checksums, but the signed manifest is the source of truth.

[15:21] Tom Wexler: Does it cover image digests too?

[15:24] Marcus Lin: Yes. Image references are pinned by digest in the manifest. So even if someone changes a tag, the digest mismatch is caught.

[15:34] Samir Qureshi: What about the model weights? Are you shipping them in the offline bundle too?

[15:39] Fatima Noor: Depending on your configuration, yes, you can include model/runtime artifacts. For some customers, they bring their own models and only install the runtime. For others, Redwood-provided model artifacts are included. Either way, anything included in the bundle is hashed and listed.

[15:58] Priya Nair: Good.

[16:00] Markus Klein: I’ll pause and see if we should walk through an example output. Fatima can share the “inspect bundle” CLI output in the follow-up doc.

[16:10] Priya Nair: Yeah, please. We want to see what an auditor would see.

[16:14] Fatima Noor: Totally.

[16:17] Tom Wexler: Failure modes: say someone copies the bundle via Windows zip and it changes line endings (we’ve seen it). How do you surface that?

[16:28] Marcus Lin: That would show up as a hash mismatch. The error includes which file failed, the expected hash, and the actual hash. And logs indicate likely causes—partial transfer, decompression tool issues, etc. We’ll include troubleshooting steps.

[16:48] Samir Qureshi: And if signature is invalid?

[16:51] Marcus Lin: You get signature_invalid, plus key id, plus “verification failed” and install blocked. Unknown_key is distinct.

[17:02] Priya Nair: Unknown key should be blocked too.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: Yes. Default is fail closed on unknown key.

[17:10] Elena Markovic: Please provide that statement explicitly.

[17:13] Marcus Lin: Will do.

[17:16] Priya Nair: Let’s talk about “initial trust.” How do we get the first public key? We will not accept “download it from your site.”

[17:26] Markus Klein: Yup. For regulated customers, we deliver the initial public key via a controlled channel. Usually that’s included in the initial onboarding package, shared through your procurement-approved mechanism, sometimes physically delivered or via your secure file transfer. We can also provide a printed fingerprint out-of-band to verify.

[17:47] Priya Nair: OK. We’ll want to verify fingerprint via a second channel.

[17:51] Markus Klein: Totally normal.

[17:54] Tom Wexler: Do you support customer-provided root keys? Like we sign and you sign? Dual control.

[18:00] Marcus Lin: Not in the initial phase. We’ve had requests for customer-signed bundles or delegated signing. It’s on the roadmap, but today we’re focused on Redwood signing plus local verification. We can document the future plan and the limitation.

[18:18] Priya Nair: Fine. We may ask for it later.

[18:22] Elena Markovic: What about third-party dependencies inside the installer? Are you scanning? Any vulnerability handling? That’s more general, but relevant.

[18:32] Olga Petrov: We do standard dependency scanning and we can provide vulnerability management process in the security package. For this project, the key is you can see what you’re installing via SBOM, and we can give release notes and patch guidance.

[18:52] Priya Nair: OK.

[18:54] Samir Qureshi: How do we export the audit events to our SIEM? We run Splunk, but offline networks have an internal forwarder.

[19:03] Fatima Noor: The Private deployment includes an audit log exporter option. It can write to local files in JSON and forward internally. We’ll share supported outputs. If you don’t run it, you still have local logs.

[19:20] Priya Nair: Local retention guidance?

[19:22] Marcus Lin: We recommend local retention aligned with your policy. We’ll provide defaults and guidance like “keep verification events at least X days” but you can set it.

[19:34] Tom Wexler: Is the verification logged only at install time, or also at upgrade?

[19:38] Fatima Noor: Both. Every time you run install/upgrade with an offline bundle, verification happens as part of preflight and it’s logged.

[19:49] Priya Nair: Can it be run standalone, like “verify without install”?

[19:53] Fatima Noor: Yes. That’s the “inspect” or “verify” command. It prints a report and exits.

[20:02] Priya Nair: Great.

[20:04] Markus Klein: We’re at ~20 minutes. Let’s do a quick structured Q&A now. Priya, anything else on supply chain?

[20:12] Priya Nair: Threat model: do you cover tampering, replay, compromised CI, compromised signing key? We’ll ask for at least a summary.

[20:22] Marcus Lin: Yes. Threat model includes tampering in transit, malicious insider in build pipeline, key compromise, and downgrade/replay. Mitigations include protected signing step, restricted access, audit logs, reproducible-ish build steps, and fail-closed verification. We can share the summary.

[20:44] Elena Markovic: And break-glass. That’s also a risk to document.

[20:48] Marcus Lin: Absolutely.

[20:50] Tom Wexler: One more technical: Kubernetes cluster has no internet. If the installer needs helm repos, it will fail. Do you package helm charts offline?

[21:00] Fatima Noor: Yes, charts are bundled as tarballs, and referenced by checksum in the manifest. No helm repo fetch.

[21:10] Tom Wexler: Good.

[21:12] Samir Qureshi: Does the bundle include a list of image digests and sizes? We sometimes need to validate media capacity.

[21:20] Fatima Noor: The manifest includes sizes for major artifacts. We also provide a “bundle info” output that shows total size and per-component breakdown.

[21:30] Priya Nair: OK.

[21:32] Markus Klein: Elena, any GRC items we didn’t cover?

[21:36] Elena Markovic: I’ll need: written statement about fail-closed, and key custody. Also, how you handle emergency unsigned hotfixes. You said break-glass for install, but do you ever ship unsigned bundles?

[21:52] Olga Petrov: Our standard is to ship signed bundles. For emergencies where signing pipeline is blocked, there is an exception process requiring approvals and customer communication. It’s very controlled. We can share the policy at a high level.

[22:11] Priya Nair: We would strongly prefer “no unsigned ever.”

[22:15] Marcus Lin: Same preference. The exception is truly break-glass and would come with explicit risk acknowledgment. Also, you could choose to refuse it.

[22:27] Tom Wexler: If we refuse, we’re down, but yes.

[22:32] Markus Klein: Right. We’ll be transparent about it.

[22:35] Priya Nair: OK.

[22:37] Markus Klein: Let’s jump to key rotation timeline. Marcus?

[22:42] Marcus Lin: In general we rotate periodically, and we can do emergency rotation. We maintain overlap: multiple trusted keys in the installer trust store. Customers update trust store before the cutover date. We’ll publish a timeline and a “not-after” date for the old key’s usage in new releases.

[23:05] Priya Nair: Again, time-based things in air gap can be tricky.

[23:09] Marcus Lin: Yeah. The time-based part is about our release policy, not your verification. Verification itself is “is this signed by a trusted key.” If you keep the old key trusted, you can still verify old signatures. The policy question is whether you *should* trust it after we say it’s compromised.

[23:29] Priya Nair: Understood.

[23:32] Samir Qureshi: For the trust store file, what format? PEM? JSON list of certs?

[23:38] Marcus Lin: Likely PEM for public keys/certs plus a small metadata wrapper (key ids). We’ll confirm. The goal is something you can manage with standard tools.

[23:51] Tom Wexler: OK.

[23:53] Markus Klein: There’s also an operational detail: support bundles. When you open a ticket, the support bundle can include “bundle verify status” and manifest metadata so Support can triage faster. That stays local unless you send it.

[24:10] Priya Nair: That’s good. Make sure no sensitive data is in it.

[24:14] Fatima Noor: Agreed. It’s mostly version/build IDs and error codes.

[24:19] Elena Markovic: Another question: do you sign the installer itself, or only the offline bundle?

[24:26] Marcus Lin: We sign the bundle artifacts; the installer binary is part of the bundle and is hashed in the signed manifest. Also, depending on OS, the installer package may have OS-level signing, but the core guarantee is via the bundle manifest signature.

[24:44] Priya Nair: OK.

[24:46] Tom Wexler: What if someone swaps the installer but leaves manifest? The hash check would catch it.

[24:51] Marcus Lin: Exactly.

[24:53] Priya Nair: Good.

[24:55] Markus Klein: Anything else on “how do we know what you built”?

[25:00] Priya Nair: If you can provide a sample manifest. Like redact if needed, but show fields.

[25:07] Fatima Noor: Yep, we can provide a sanitized sample.

[25:10] Markus Klein: Great.

[25:12] (crosstalk)

[25:13] Samir Qureshi: Sorry one more. Do you support verifying without extracting the entire bundle? Sometimes we want to check on the jump host.

[25:22] Fatima Noor: Verification needs access to the manifest and signature and either the artifact files or their checksums, so practically you need it extracted or mounted. But we can verify the signature quickly without full extraction, then do hashes as a second step.

[25:41] Samir Qureshi: OK.

[25:44] Markus Klein: Let’s take 2 minutes—Priya, do you want to mention any of your internal constraints? Like no outbound DNS, no NTP, etc.

[25:55] Priya Nair: Yeah. No outbound anything. Time is from an internal time source but it’s not guaranteed on every host. We can’t rely on public CAs. And we need to store logs locally for 1 year.

[26:10] Marcus Lin: Helpful. We’ll add guidance: if system time is bad, how to remediate, and what our signature verification expects.

[26:20] Tom Wexler: Also, we run OpenShift in one environment and vanilla Kubernetes in another.

[26:26] Fatima Noor: Fine. Offline bundle approach is consistent across both.

[26:31] Markus Klein: Great.

[26:33] Elena Markovic: You mentioned competitors earlier—just for context, we’re also evaluating AWS Bedrock private link and Azure OpenAI in a dedicated region. But they still require network. So you’re the only air-gap option in this set.

[26:48] Markus Klein: Yep, makes sense.

[26:50] Priya Nair: OK, I think we’re good. Let’s do a quick recap.

[26:55] Markus Klein: Sure. Recap: Offline bundle includes all required artifacts, manifest lists hashes, manifest is signed, verification is offline and fail-closed by default. Unknown key blocks. We have trust store and key rotation with overlap and offline update steps. Audit events are emitted locally and can be exported. Break-glass is documented and noisy.

[27:22] Priya Nair: Please send: sample manifest, sample verification output, and written statement about fail closed and unknown key behavior. Also key custody narrative.

[27:33] Olga Petrov: We’ll send a TPRM-friendly packet.

[27:36] Marcus Lin: And I’ll answer the crypto algorithm question once we confirm your allowed list.

[27:43] Tom Wexler: Great.

[27:45] Markus Klein: Perfect. We’ll schedule a 30-min follow-up once you’ve reviewed. Thanks everyone.

[27:52] (call ends - recording continued with minor silence)

[28:10] Fireflies.ai Note: Some audio after 27:52 contained silence/side conversation not captured.
